### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

English

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

Two sentences, from Lecture VI, “Pragmatism's Conception of Truth,” in Pragmatism (1907). The second sentence is what the first means.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Truth happens to an idea.”
-   “Truth is what happens to an idea.”

### Attribution notes

Quoted at the first sentence alone it reads as relativism — as if anything could become true. James' argument is the opposite: an idea is made true by its verification in events, so the second sentence is not an elaboration but the claim itself. Cutting it off is the single most common way this passage is misrepresented, and readers who arrive looking for the source are usually looking because the one-sentence version seemed to say something James would have denied.

#### About William James

William James (1842–1910) was the Harvard psychologist-philosopher who popularized pragmatism and pioneered scientific psychology in America. Brother of novelist Henry James, he trained in medicine and wrote The Principles of Psychology and The Varieties of Religious Experience.

### Interpretation

This is the core of James's theory of truth and the sentence most often quoted out of his argument. He is denying that an idea is true by corresponding to a ready-made reality and proposing instead that truth is something that happens to an idea when acting on it works out. "Made true by events" means verification is a process in time, not a property an idea already has. Critics have argued this conflates truth with usefulness, and James spent later lectures trying to answer that objection.

#### Why it matters

The practical version: treat a belief as a hypothesis whose value is shown by where acting on it leads. That stance makes revision cheaper, since being wrong is information rather than a defeat.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true,…”?

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true,…” comes from Pragmatism, attributed to William James.

#### What does William James mean by truth?

Correspondence, coherence, pragmatist, and deflationary theories compete. Ethics and politics ask who gets to define truth in public life. This passage enters that discussion through truth, action.

#### Is the wording of this William James quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.” Forms in circulation that differ: Truth happens to an idea. / Truth is what happens to an idea. The English reads “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Quoted at the first sentence alone it reads as relativism — as if anything could become true. James' argument is the opposite: an idea is made true by its verification in events, so the second sentence is not an elaboration but the claim itself. Cutting it off is the single most common way this passage is misrepresented, and readers who arrive looking for the source are usually looking because the one-sentence version seemed to say something James would have denied.
